name: Apollo 17
short_status: Landed at Taurus-Littrow December 11, 1972; last crewed Moon landing, splashed down December 19, 1972.
tagline: NASA · United States · Crewed landing · 1972 · The space race Success

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 7 December 1972, 12:33 a.m. EST from Pad 39A, the first US crewed night launch

facts.label: Crew
facts.value: Eugene A. Cernan (Commander), Ronald E. Evans (Command Module Pilot, CSM America), Harrison H. Schmitt (Lunar Module Pilot, LM Challenger), the first scientist-astronaut and first trained geologist on the Moon

facts.label: Lunar landing
facts.value: 11 December 1972, 2:55 p.m. EST (19:54:57 UTC), Taurus-Littrow valley on the southeast edge of Mare Serenitatis, about 200 m east of the planned point

facts.label: LM coordinates (LROC-derived)
facts.value: 20.1911 N, 30.7723 E, uncertainty ±3.5 m, statistical mean of repeated LROC NAC imaging 2009-2015

facts.label: Surface stay
facts.value: 75 hours, the longest of Apollo; three EVAs totaling 22 h 4 m (7:12, 7:37, 7:15), with EVA-2 the longest single Apollo moonwalk

facts.label: Samples
facts.value: 110.4 kg (243 lb), the most of any Apollo mission; NASA history pages quote 254 lb, a known discrepancy

facts.label: Rover distance
facts.value: 22.2 miles (35.7 km) driven on the third LRV per NASA history; NASA's mission-details page lists the traverse as 30.5 km

facts.label: Orange soil
facts.value: Discovered by Schmitt at Shorty crater (Station 4, EVA-2, 12-13 December 1972); sample 74220's beads are high-titanium volcanic glass from fire-fountain sprays about 3.5 billion years ago

facts.label: Last steps
facts.value: Cernan was the last person to leave footprints on the Moon; Schmitt was the twelfth and final person to step onto it. EVA-3 ended in the early hours of 14 December 1972 UTC

facts.label: Liftoff from the Moon
facts.value: 14 December 1972, 10:54:37 p.m. GMT (5:54 p.m. EST); per NASA history, the last word transmitted from the surface was Schmitt's "Ignition"

facts.label: Trans-Earth EVA
facts.value: Ron Evans spent 1 h 6 m outside CSM America during the coast home, retrieving the Lunar Sounder, Panoramic Camera, and Mapping Camera film cassettes

facts.label: Splashdown
facts.value: 19 December 1972, Pacific Ocean near American Samoa, under 4 miles from USS Ticonderoga; mission duration 12 days 13 h 52 m

facts.label: Artemis I anniversary tie
facts.value: Orion's Artemis I splashdown on 11 December 2022 (9:40 a.m. PST, after 25.5 days) came 50 years to the day after Apollo 17's Moon landing

facts.label: Successor
facts.value: Artemis II (1-10 April 2026) was the first crewed flight beyond low Earth orbit since Apollo 17; the next crewed landing is slated for Artemis IV

timeline: Launch at 12:33 a.m. EST, the first US crewed night launch; the Blue Marble photo of Earth is taken during translunar coast
Challenger lands at Taurus-Littrow at 2:55 p.m. EST, about 200 m east of the planned point
EVA-1 (7 h 12 m): ALSEP deployed about 600 ft west-northwest of the LM; 2 miles driven, nearly 32 lb of samples
EVA-2 (7 h 37 m), the longest Apollo moonwalk with a 20.4 km round trip; Schmitt finds the orange soil at Shorty crater
EVA-3 (7 h 15 m) ends with Cernan taking humanity's last steps on the Moon to date
Challenger lifts off at 10:54:37 p.m. GMT after a 7 m 18 s ascent burn; Schmitt's "Ignition" is the last word transmitted from the surface
Trans-Earth coast: Evans' 1 h 6 m deep-space EVA to retrieve three SIM-bay film cassettes
Splashdown near American Samoa, under 4 miles from USS Ticonderoga; 12 d 13 h 52 m total, the end of Apollo lunar exploration
Artemis I's Orion splashes down 50 years to the day after the Apollo 17 landing
Artemis II carries four astronauts around the Moon, the first humans beyond low Earth orbit since Apollo 17
